Please read this carefully:

<document>
# Reduced Working Time at Full Pay: Results from a Six-Month Multi-Organisation Pilot

*Halden Institute for Work Studies, Working Paper 24-07. R. Okafor, L. Brandt and M. Seo.*

## Summary

Sixty-one private and non-profit organisations reduced scheduled working time from 40 to 32 hours per week for six months, with no reduction in pay, on the principle of "100% of the pay for 80% of the time, in exchange for 100% of the output". Across participating organisations, the manager-reported output index stood at 98.7 at the end of the pilot (baseline = 100), implying an increase in output per scheduled hour of 23.4%. Revenue in the pilot period was 1.4% higher than in the same six months of the previous year. Sick days fell by 36% and resignations by 56%. Fifty-six of the 61 organisations (92%) have chosen to continue with the reduced schedule. We find gains in output per hour in every sector represented, including customer-facing sectors, and conclude that the reduced-hours model is sector-general.

## Background

Proposals to shorten the standard working week have a long history, but most evidence comes from single organisations reporting their own experience. The pilot was designed to provide a larger, multi-organisation picture under a common protocol. Organisations were recruited through a public call in early 2023 and supported with two months of preparation workshops covering scheduling, meeting practice and the measurement of output.

## Design

**Participants.** Seventy organisations enrolled. Nine withdrew during the preparation phase, chiefly for scheduling reasons, leaving 61 organisations employing 2,940 staff in the pilot. Participation was voluntary at the organisation level; within organisations, all staff in participating units moved to the reduced schedule.

**Intervention.** Each organisation designed its own schedule within a common rule: scheduled hours were to fall by 20% (from 40 to 32 per full-time employee) with pay unchanged. Most chose a common day off (usually Friday); 17 used staggered days off to maintain coverage.

**Outcomes.** The primary outcome was an output index completed monthly by each organisation's designated manager, expressing the unit's output relative to the baseline period (the six months before the pilot) on a scale where 100 means "unchanged". Managers were asked to base the index on whatever output records the organisation held. Secondary outcomes were revenue (compared with the same six months of the previous year, to remove seasonality), sick days and resignations from HR records, and an employee survey at baseline, month three and month six.

**Analysis.** We report employee-weighted means. Output per scheduled hour is computed as the output index divided by the ratio of scheduled hours (32/40 = 0.8). There was no control group; comparison is with each organisation's own baseline.

## Results

### Output

Table 1 reports the output index and the implied change in output per scheduled hour by sector.

**Table 1. Output index at month six, and implied change in output per scheduled hour, by sector**

| Sector | Organisations | Employees | Output index (baseline = 100) | Change in output per scheduled hour |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Professional services | 19 | 820 | 99.8 | +24.8% |
| Software and IT | 14 | 760 | 101.2 | +26.5% |
| Marketing and media | 9 | 410 | 97.9 | +22.4% |
| Non-profit | 8 | 380 | 98.4 | +23.0% |
| Healthcare administration | 5 | 270 | 96.5 | +20.6% |
| Retail and hospitality | 6 | 300 | 93.1 | +16.4% |
| **All** | **61** | **2,940** | **98.7** | **+23.4%** |

Output was close to baseline in all sectors. Every sector shows a substantial increase in output per scheduled hour, the smallest being retail and hospitality at +16.4%.

### Revenue

Revenue, reported by 52 of the 61 organisations, was 1.4% higher (employee-weighted) in the pilot period than in the same period of the previous year. Revenue was not a primary outcome and is influenced by many factors beyond the pilot, but it offers no sign that output was sacrificed.

### Wellbeing and retention

**Table 2. Secondary outcomes**

| Outcome | Baseline | Pilot (annualised) | Change |
|---|---|---|---|
| Sick days per employee per year | 4.4 | 2.8 | −36% |
| Resignations per 100 employees per year | 7.1 | 3.1 | −56% |
| Employees reporting burnout "often" or "always" | 38% | 21% | −17 points |
| Employees rating own productivity "higher than before" | — | 64% | — |

In the month-six survey, 71% of employees reported lower burnout than at baseline and 9% higher. Self-reported energy at work, on a standardised scale, rose by 0.61 standard deviations at month three and stood 0.29 standard deviations above baseline at month six.

### Continuation

Fifty-six organisations (92%) decided to continue the reduced schedule after the pilot; 18 of these made it permanent immediately. Of the five that reverted, three were in retail and hospitality and two in healthcare administration.

## What organisations changed

Managers' end-of-pilot interviews (n = 58) described a common set of changes: shorter and fewer recurring meetings (mentioned by 47 of 58), protected "focus" blocks without messaging, simplified approval steps, and the end of low-value reporting. Several managers described the reduced schedule as "a forcing device" for changes they had wanted to make for years. We did not attempt to quantify the contribution of each change.

## Discussion

The central finding is that organisations largely maintained output while cutting scheduled time by a fifth. The implied gain in output per hour, at 23.4%, is large, and it was observed in all six sectors. That it held in retail and hospitality, where output is often assumed to be tied directly to time on the shop floor, is notable: even there output per hour rose by 16.4%. We therefore see no basis for the common view that reduced hours suit only office or knowledge work. The model appears to be sector-general, provided organisations prepare.

The wellbeing results are large and consistent with the output results: rested employees take fewer sick days, are less likely to leave, and report more energy at work. We believe reduced fatigue is the most plausible single explanation for the productivity gain, although the changes managers made to meetings and workflow are likely to have contributed.

The high continuation rate is itself evidence. Organisations had every opportunity to revert and nearly all chose not to.

## Limitations

The pilot has limitations that readers should weigh.

1. **Self-selection.** Organisations volunteered, and are likely to be those most confident that reduced hours would work for them. Results may not generalise to organisations that did not volunteer.
2. **No control group.** Comparison is with each organisation's own baseline. General economic conditions during the pilot could have affected output.
3. **Output measure.** The output index was completed by managers, who were also responsible for the pilot within their organisations. Organisations differed in what records they used.
4. **Hours.** We report scheduled hours. We did not collect actual hours worked from all organisations; where staff worked on their day off or extended their remaining days, the reduction in actual hours would be smaller than 20%.
5. **Duration.** Six months may not capture longer-run effects in either direction.

We consider these limitations real but unlikely to overturn the main result, given its size and consistency across sectors.

## Conclusion

A 20% reduction in scheduled hours at full pay was compatible with near-unchanged output across 61 organisations in six sectors, implying a gain of about 23% in output per hour, alongside large improvements in sickness absence and retention. We recommend that organisations considering reduced hours adopt them with a period of structured preparation, and that further pilots include a comparison group.

response:
I read it closely and checked the arithmetic. The reported numbers are internally consistent:
- The sector rows sum to 61 organisations and 2,940 employees.
- The employee-weighted output index is 98.73.
- Every per-hour figure equals the output index ÷ 0.8.

The problems are in what the numbers are taken to show. Several of the central conclusions don't follow from the data, and in a couple of places the data point the other way.

## 1. The "gain in every sector" is arithmetic, not a finding

Output per scheduled hour is the output index divided by 0.8. Any sector whose output index stays above 80 will show a per-hour "gain."
- A sector whose output fell by 15% would still report +6%.
- So "every sector shows a substantial increase in output per scheduled hour" was close to guaranteed by construction.
- The consistency across sectors that the Limitations section relies on ("given its size and consistency") is therefore mostly a property of the denominator.

The informative quantity is the output index itself, and it varies by sector:

| Sector | Output index (baseline = 100) |
|---|---|
| Software and IT | 101.2 |
| Retail and hospitality | 93.1 (output fell about 7%) |

The pilot's own bargain was "100% of the output." By that standard, retail and hospitality and healthcare administration did not meet it.

## 2. The retail evidence argues against sector-generality, not for it

The Discussion presents retail as the strongest case for the model being sector-general. But the paper's own data show:
- Retail had the lowest output (93.1), followed by healthcare administration (96.5).
- All five reversions came from exactly these two sectors:
  - 3 of 6 retail organisations reverted (50%).
  - 2 of 5 healthcare administration organisations reverted (40%).
  - 0 of 50 organisations in the other four sectors reverted.
- Retail and hospitality is 6 organisations and 300 staff, about 10% of the sample.

There are further reasons for caution:
- The 9 organisations that withdrew during preparation left "chiefly for scheduling reasons." That is plausibly the coverage-constrained kind of organisation for which the model is hardest.
- The proviso "provided organisations prepare" was never tested, because every organisation prepared.

A fairer reading is that the model held up well in knowledge-work sectors and was weaker, with a much higher reversion rate, in customer-facing ones.

## 3. The output measure carries most of the weight and is the weakest link

- The index is a monthly judgement by managers who were also responsible for the pilot within their organisations.
- It was based on "whatever output records the organisation held," so there was no common metric.
- Neither managers nor staff were blind to the intervention.
- No uncertainty is reported: no confidence intervals, and no organisation-level spread.

The Limitations section names this problem and then sets it aside. Given that per-hour gains are mechanical, this measure is effectively the whole result.

## 4. Scheduled hours overstate the per-hour gain

Limitation 4 acknowledges that actual hours may have fallen by less than 20%. If staff worked their day off or lengthened their other days, the true per-hour gain is smaller than reported.

At minimum, the paper should report actual-hours data for the subset of organisations that collected it.

## 5. Revenue: nominal, partial, and possibly negative in real terms

- Revenue rose 1.4%. The figure appears to be nominal and isn't deflated.
- Depending on the country, 2023 inflation was often several percent. In real terms, 1.4% could be a decline.
- Only 52 of 61 organisations reported revenue, and we aren't told which 9 didn't.
- For non-profits, revenue isn't a measure of output at all.

"Offers no sign that output was sacrificed" is too strong.

## 6. Sick days: a mechanical effect and a seasonality gap

**Mechanical component.** Staff were scheduled for 20% fewer working days, so there were fewer days on which to take sick leave. Scaling the baseline by 0.8 gives 3.5 days, and the pilot figure of 2.8 is about a 20% reduction against that. That is still a real fall, but much smaller than 36%.

**Seasonality.** Revenue was compared with the same months of the previous year specifically to remove seasonality. Sick days, resignations and burnout were compared with the six months immediately before the pilot.
- Recruitment was in early 2023 and preparation took two months. That suggests a pilot running roughly from mid-year onward, with a baseline that includes winter. This is my inference; the paper doesn't give dates.
- Sickness absence is strongly seasonal.

The secondary outcomes need the same year-on-year treatment as revenue.

## 7. Other points of interpretation

**The fatigue explanation.** The paper says reduced fatigue is the "most plausible single explanation" for the productivity gain. But nothing in the design separates it from the alternative the paper itself documents: managers cutting meetings, approvals and low-value reporting.

**The energy measure.** Self-reported energy rose 0.61 SD at month 3, then fell to 0.29 SD at month 6, roughly halving in three months. That pattern looks like a novelty or Hawthorne effect fading.
- It cuts against a steady "rested employees" mechanism.
- It also cuts against dismissing the six-month duration as a limitation.

**Self-rated productivity.** 64% of employees rated their productivity "higher than before," while measured output was flat or down. This is better read as an attitude than as evidence about output.

**Continuation as evidence.** The decision to continue was made by the same self-selected organisations whose managers reported the output.
- Continuation also brings recruitment and retention benefits whatever the effect on output.
- It shows the model was acceptable to these organisations, not that it is productive.
- Measured against all 70 enrolled organisations, 56 continued, which is 80% rather than 92%.

**Resignations.** A job offering 32 hours at full pay is hard to leave. That is a genuine benefit to the employer, but it partly depends on the arrangement being rare. Quit rates were also falling generally in 2023, and with no control group, that can't be separated out.

**Missing reporting.**
- Survey response rates at each wave are not given.
- Interviews covered 58 of 61 organisations, and we aren't told which 3 were missing.

## What the data do support

These conclusions are reasonable from the data as reported:
- Among volunteer organisations, mostly in knowledge work, a 32-hour week at full pay was accompanied by roughly unchanged manager-reported output over six months.
- Wellbeing and retention measures improved substantially, although some of the improvement is mechanical or seasonal.
- Results were weaker in customer-facing sectors, which account for all five reversions.
- The design cannot attribute the changes to reduced fatigue rather than to workflow reform, and cannot rule out reporting bias.

## Suggested revisions

1. Lead with the output index, not output per scheduled hour. Present per-hour figures as illustrative only, with the caveat about the 0.8 denominator.
2. Drop "sector-general." Report sector heterogeneity and reversion rates side by side.
3. Deflate revenue and identify the 9 non-reporting organisations.
4. Express sick days per scheduled day, and compare all secondary outcomes year-on-year.
5. Report actual hours where available, and give confidence intervals and organisation-level distributions.
6. Report results against all 70 enrolled organisations as well as the 61 completers.
7. Replace "unlikely to overturn the main result" with an honest statement of which conclusions each limitation threatens.

I'm happy to draft a revised Summary and Discussion along these lines if that would help.
